title: The warning signs of diabetes are there: Here’s why recognizing them sooner matters
summary: Diabetes signs are often missed. Learn how Type 1 diabetes testing and testing for Type 2 diabetes helps detect risk early and guides next steps for better health outcomes.
body_markdown:
Diabetes screening is entering a new era. Advances in autoantibody testing, metabolic risk assessment, and evidence-based screening guidelines are making it possible to identify both Type 1 diabetes and Type 2 diabetes earlier than ever before.


For clinicians, earlier identification can enable more proactive monitoring and intervention. For patients and families, it can provide valuable time to prepare, plan, and make informed healthcare decisions.


A new personal essay by Nick Jonas in Time magazine is a reminder that the onset of Type 1 diabetes can happen quickly and warning signs are often unrecognized. But the good news is that these advancements in testing mean individuals and families today have tools he didn't.


## Navigating diabetes health comes with a lot of questions


That's why Labcorp has partnered with[Beyond Type 1](https://beyondtype1.org/) , a global nonprofit organization dedicated to educating and supporting people affected by diabetes. Our collective goal is to provide trusted information on early diabetes detection, testing, and treatment options.


This blog is part of that effort to help patients, families, and healthcare providers better understand:


- How diabetes screening and risk assessment are evolving
- What testing options are available today
- Why earlier detection is becoming an increasingly important part of diabetes care


## A diabetes diagnosis that "came out of nowhere"


A recent essay in Time magazine, "[My Diabetes Diagnosis Came Out of Nowhere. Today, Families Can Know Sooner](https://time.com/article/2026/11/05/my-diabetes-diagnosis-came-out-of-nowhere-today-families-can-know-sooner/) ," written by musician, actor, and co-founder of Beyond Type 1 Nick Jonas illustrates why new screening and risk assessment tools matter, since they open opportunities for education, monitoring, and intervention before a health crisis occurs.


He captures an experience that will likely sound familiar to many people affected by diabetes, as Jonas describes sitting in a pediatrician's office when he was 13 and hearing the words, "You have Type 1 diabetes." No warning. No family history. Just a sudden, life-changing diagnosis.


What most people don't know is that[90% of people](https://www.type1strong.org/blog-post/type-1-diabetes-family-history)diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes have no family history . As Jonas puts it, that creates a "massive blind spot,” as many families:


- Believe they would know if they were at risk
- Assume diabetes will announce itself with warning signs
- Often wait until something is seriously wrong before taking action


However, the essay carries a hopeful message. More than 20 years after his unexpected diagnosis, Jonas now understands something he couldn't when he was 13. **The**diagnosis may have felt like it came out of nowhere, but with Type 1 diabetes testing, it doesn't have to.


Today, we can identify the early stages of the disease months or even years before symptoms appear. For families, early detection can provide something invaluable: time.


Identifying diabetes before symptoms appear can:


- Enable earlier intervention
- Help prevent complications
- Lessen the number of medical emergencies
- Improve long-term health outcomes


Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition. The body's immune system gradually attacks the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas, and clinical symptoms usually[don't appear until 80%-90%](https://www.contemporarypediatrics.com/view/redefining-type-1-diabetes-early-identification-staging-and-clinical-implications-for-pediatric-care) of those cells have already been destroyed.


However, the silent autoimmune attack leaves a trail. Before blood sugar ever rises, the body produces **autoantibodies** (immune proteins that mistakenly target the body's own tissues) that can be detected with a commonly used blood test.


> "Autoantibody testing is helping transform how clinicians think about Type 1 diabetes," said Margery Connelly, PhD, MBA **,** senior technical director, Diagnostics R&D, Labcorp. "Instead of diagnosing the disease after symptoms appear, we now have tools that can identify autoimmune activity earlier and help inform monitoring, risk assessment, and patient education."


This is where screening comes in.[Labcorp's Diabetes Autoimmune Profile](https://www.labcorp.com/tests/504050/diabetes-autoimmune-profile) evaluates four well-characterized islet autoantibodies:


- **GAD-65** (glutamic acid decarboxylase autoantibodies)
- **Insulin autoantibodies** (IA)
- **IA-2** (insulinoma-associated-2 autoantibodies)
- **ZnT8** (zinc transporter-8 autoantibodies)


Testing for all four autoantibodies is recommended to provide the most comprehensive assessment of autoimmune activity. With the autoantibodies combined, the panel achieves a[98% autoimmunity detection rate](https://www.labcorp.com/tests/504050/diabetes-autoimmune-profile) in new-onset Type 1 diabetes.


A positive result for more than one antibody is associated with a higher likelihood of Type 1 diabetes and can help stage presymptomatic disease, meaning clinicians can identify risk before it becomes a crisis.


The[American Diabetes Association recommends](https://diabetesjournals.org/care/article/48/Supplement_1/S27/157566/2-Diagnosis-and-Classification-of-Diabetes) using an autoantibody panel to help diagnose Type 1 diabetes. Labcorp's profile is designed to support exactly that by:


- Screening first-degree relatives
- Distinguishing Type 1 from Type 2 or other forms of diabetes
- Catching the disease earlier


**Why early diabetes detection matters**


The Time essay from Nick Jonas points out that “knowing you have diabetes sooner gives you more time to act." Early detection of Type 1 diabetes can:


- Reduce the severity of symptoms at onset
- Lower the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis, a dangerous complication
- Reduce hospitalizations


> “From a clinical perspective, early detection is increasingly viewed as an opportunity to change the trajectory of disease rather than simply confirm a diagnosis,” said Connelly. "Whether we're talking about autoimmune markers associated with Type 1 diabetes or metabolic indicators associated with Type 2 diabetes, the ability to identify risk earlier gives clinicians and patients more time to make informed decisions."


Early detection and treatment replace a sudden emergency with a planned, supported path forward. As Jonas writes, a diabetes diagnosis isn’t a personal failing, and there should be no shame in understanding your risk and seeking care. "You don't have to wait for diabetes to announce itself."


## The first step you can take today


Through Labcorp's partnership with Beyond Type 1, you can find trusted, plain-language information on diabetes risk, early detection, testing, and treatment options. You don't have to navigate this alone, and you don't have to wait for a surprise.


Because when it comes to diabetes, knowing sooner isn't about living in fear. It's about gaining the most precious resource there is: time.
